title: Edit Distance (Levenshtein)
description: Minimum insert/delete/replace edits to turn word1 into word2. 2D DP: dp[i][j] = edits between word1[:i] and word2[:j]. Match → carry diagonal; mismatch → 1 + min(insert, delete, replace).

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: given two strings `word1` and `word2`, return the minimum number of single-character operations to convert `word1` into `word2`. Operations are insert, delete, and replace — each costs 1."

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Are the three operations equally weighted at 1, or do they have different costs?
• Case-sensitive? ('Apple' vs 'apple' — 1 edit or 0?)
• ASCII or Unicode? (Affects whether `word1[i]` indexes bytes or code units.)
• Empty strings on either side — convert empty to length-`n` is `n` inserts, right?
• Length bounds — is `O(m·n)` time/space acceptable?
sections.why: The equal-cost question matters because weighted edit distance changes the recurrence (each `+1` becomes a per-op cost). Most problem statements assume cost-1 but it's worth confirming. The empty-string question pins down the base row/column: `dp[0][j] = j` (insert all of `word2`) and `dp[i][0] = i` (delete all of `word1`). Pinning down `O(m·n)` upfront preempts the space-optimization pushback — if `m·n` is too big they want you to know about the rolling-row trick.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious exponential solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is recursive: compare the last chars of both strings. If they match, recurse on `(m-1, n-1)` with no cost. If they don't, return `1 + min(recurse(m-1, n), recurse(m, n-1), recurse(m-1, n-1))` — the three branches correspond to delete from `word1`, insert into `word1`, replace. Base cases: empty `word1` returns `n` (insert all), empty `word2` returns `m` (delete all). That's `O(3^min(m,n))` worst case — three-way branching, depth `min(m,n)`. Massive overlap on `(i,j)` subproblems; memoization brings it to `O(m·n)`."
sections.why: The three-way recursive split is what plants the recurrence — once you say 'mismatch means try all three ops, take the cheapest, add one', the bottom-up table is just memoizing the recursion in reverse. The 'characters match → no cost, carry diagonal' clause is the load-bearing detail; missing it leads to an off-by-one where matches still cost 1. Naming it in recursion first makes the bottom-up version feel like a translation, not a leap.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to 2D bottom-up tabulation?
sections.say:
"This is classic 2D DP over prefix pairs. The recurrence: `dp[i][j]` = min edits to turn `word1[0..i)` into `word2[0..j)`. The decision at each step is what to do with the *last* character of each prefix:
• If `word1[i-1] === word2[j-1]`, the last chars already agree, no op needed — inherit the diagonal: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]`.
• Otherwise, take 1 plus the minimum of the three predecessors: `dp[i-1][j] + 1` (delete from `word1`), `dp[i][j-1] + 1` (insert into `word1`), `dp[i-1][j-1] + 1` (replace).

Base cases live in row 0 and column 0: `dp[i][0] = i` (delete `i` chars), `dp[0][j] = j` (insert `j` chars). Answer sits at `dp[m][n]`. The `(m+1) × (n+1)` table is what lets the base row/column live at index 0 cleanly."
sections.why: Articulating the *three operations as three table neighbors* — delete is top, insert is left, replace is diagonal — is the load-bearing pedagogy. Once that mapping clicks, the recurrence is mechanical: 'I'm at `(i,j)`; I either spent zero ops to inherit the diagonal (chars matched) or I spent one to do one of the three things'. The off-by-one between string index `i-1` and table index `i` is the easy trap — always say it out loud so the interviewer sees you're tracking it.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a single replace, a single insert, and a multi-op case that exercises all three operations.

examples.note: One substitute (a→u). Diagonal carries match for c and t; only the middle column triggers an op.
Single insert at the end. Diagonal carries through ab; the extra c is one left-step (insert).
Three ops total — one replace (h→r) and two deletes (r and e). All three operations show up in the optimal path.
examples.trace:
init table (6×4), first row/col are 0..n / 0..m
Walking just the answer path:
dp[5][3] = 3, reached via:
  - replace h→r (cost 1)
  - keep o (match)
  - keep r→s? No, r doesn't match s. Need: delete r, keep s, delete e
The key cells: dp[1][1]=1 (h→r replace), dp[2][2]=1 (carry diag, o==o is one mismatch ago but ros has 'o' second... walk shows dp fills to dp[5][3]=3.
Final: dp[5][3] = 3

sections.why: Tracing the table surfaces three things. (1) The `cat→cut` case shows match carries the diagonal cleanly — the answer is one because c and t both gave 'free' diagonal passes, only the middle paid. (2) `ab→abc` shows the insert (left-neighbor) operation in isolation. (3) The off-by-one between table index `i` and string index `i-1` is the bug that bites — saying it out loud while you trace is what catches it before you code.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Both empty — `dp[0][0] = 0`, answer is 0. ✓
• One empty — `dp[m][0] = m` or `dp[0][n] = n`, exactly the other length. The base row/column handles this without any branching.
• Identical strings — every diagonal carries, no op fires, returns 0.
• Completely disjoint strings (e.g. "abc" → "xyz") — every cell mismatches; the answer is `max(m, n)` (replace all the overlapping chars, then insert/delete the rest).
• Very different lengths (e.g. "a" → "abcdef") — answer is `|m - n| + matches lost = 5`. Handled by the recurrence; the base row pre-fills the high-cost edge.
• Unicode — `word1[i]` indexes UTF-16 code units, not code points, so an emoji compared as one char would read as two halves. If the spec mentions emoji, use `[...word1]` and index that array instead.
• Huge inputs — `O(m·n)` time and space can blow memory at `m·n ~ 10^7`. The rolling-row trick drops space to `O(min(m, n))` by keeping only two rows."
sections.why: The disjoint-strings answer (`max(m, n)`) is a clean sanity check the interviewer can verify mentally — naming it shows you've reasoned about the bound, not just trusted the table. The Unicode call-out is the senior signal — most candidates assume ASCII; flagging emoji handling (and the `[...word]` fix) demonstrates real string-internals awareness. The rolling-row space optimization is the standard 'can you do better than O(m·n) space?' follow-up answer.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is `O(m·n)` — `(m+1)(n+1)` cells, constant work per cell (one comparison, at most three lookups, one min). Space is `O(m·n)` for the full table.

The naive recursive version was `O(3^min(m,n))` time; memoization brings it to `O(m·n)` time / `O(m·n)` space; bottom-up tabulation keeps the same bounds with smaller constants. The space optimization: since each cell only reads the previous row (top, diagonal) and the current row (left), you only need two rows in memory — drops space to `O(min(m, n))` by always making the smaller dimension the inner loop.

If the interviewer asks for the actual edit sequence (not just the count), I'd add backpointers — each cell records which of the four predecessors it came from, then walk back from `dp[m][n]` to `dp[0][0]` and emit the corresponding ops in reverse. That's still `O(m·n)` time / `O(m·n)` space (can't compress with backpointers).

Template variants: Longest Common Subsequence (same 2D shape, max instead of min, no replace op); Distinct Subsequences (count rather than min); Wildcard Matching and Regex Matching (string-vs-pattern variants with different match rules). All share the prefix-pair 2D table."
sections.why: Defending both the standard and the rolling-row bound demonstrates you know the space optimization without having to be prompted. The 'recover the actual sequence' note is the natural follow-up; naming the backpointer trick proves you've thought past the count-only spec. The LCS/Distinct Subseq/Regex Matching extensions prove you see the 2D prefix-pair shape as a template — that family of problems is wide, and recognizing it is what lets you skip the derivation on the next variant.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the (m+1)×(n+1) Levenshtein table. Row 0 / column 0 hold base cases (i deletes / j inserts). For each interior cell: match carries the diagonal, mismatch is 1 + min(top, left, diagonal).
trace: function* trace(input) {
const { word1: w1, word2: w2 } = input;
yield { line: 1, label: `enter — w1="${w1}", w2="${w2}"`, state: { w1, w2 } };
const m = w1.length, n = w2.length;
const dp = Array.from({ length: m + 1 }, () => new Array(n + 1).fill(0));
const snap = () => dp.map(row => row.slice());
yield { line: 4, label: `allocate (${m + 1})x(${n + 1}) dp table, all zeros`, state: { w1, w2, m, n, dp: snap() } };
for (let i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;
yield { line: 6, label: `base col 0: dp[i][0] = i (i deletes to reach empty)`, state: { w1, w2, dp: snap() } };
for (let j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;
yield { line: 7, label: `base row 0: dp[0][j] = j (j inserts from empty)`, state: { w1, w2, dp: snap() } };
for (let i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
for (let j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
const a = w1[i - 1], b = w2[j - 1];
if (a === b) {
yield { line: 12, label: `dp[${i}][${j}] '${a}'=='${b}' → carry diag dp[${i - 1}][${j - 1}]=${dp[i][j]}`, state: { w1, w2, i, j, dp: snap(), lastFilled: [i, j] } };
} else {
const top = dp[i - 1][j], left = dp[i][j - 1], diag = dp[i - 1][j - 1];
dp[i][j] = 1 + Math.min(top, left, diag);
yield { line: 14, label: `dp[${i}][${j}] '${a}'!='${b}' → 1 + min(del=${top}, ins=${left}, repl=${diag}) = ${dp[i][j]}`, state: { w1, w2, i, j, dp: snap(), lastFilled: [i, j] } };
yield { line: 22, label: `return dp[${m}][${n}] = ${dp[m][n]}`, state: { w1, w2, dp: snap(), returns: dp[m][n] } };

notes: Row 0 and column 0 are the base cases: converting to/from the empty string costs exactly the other length.
On a character match the cost CARRIES from dp[i-1][j-1] — no +1.
The three predecessors map to delete (top), insert (left), replace (diagonal). Take min, then add one.

questions.q: Why is dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j?
options: It's a sentinel row/column used to detect when a recurrence reads out of bounds
Converting to/from the empty string costs exactly that many edits
It anchors the diagonal so dp[i-1][j-1] never reads undefined when i or j is 1
i and j are the indices of the last matched character in each prefix

questions.q: On a character match (w1[i-1] === w2[j-1]) the recurrence is:
Which DP neighbors correspond to the three edit operations?
options: Top = replace, Left = match, Diagonal = delete
Top = delete, Left = insert, Diagonal = replace
Top = insert, Left = delete, Diagonal = match
Top = delete, Left = replace, Diagonal = insert

questions.q: Time and space complexity of the standard 2D DP?
questions.explain: Space CAN be O(min(m,n)) with rolling rows, but the canonical 2D table is O(m*n).

blanks.hint: i deletes turn w1[:i] into empty
j inserts build w2[:j] from empty
one edit on top of the best neighbor
